newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ex-communist judge controversially promoted.
newsitem.headline: German ex-communist judge controversially promoted.

text.p: A former East German law professor with a classic "apparatchik" past was given a prestigious judicial post on Wednesday in the eastern state of Brandenburg.
The appointment demonstrated how Germany is still struggling to come to terms with the communist influence in the region.
The Brandenburg state assembly voted overwhelmingly to place Rosemarie Will, 47, on the state's constitutional court, making her the first former communist jurist to achieve such status.
The state's ruling Social Democrats (SPD) said her promotion showed there was a place in a united Germany for easterners, who often complain of being politically and economically shut out.
But conservatives and former dissidents felt her appointment was an affront to thousands of victims of the totalitarian east German system she believed in and helped to uphold.

"This is a judge who made a decisive contribution to the development of East German injustice. It's a scandal," said Angelika Barbe, a founder of the SPD in East Germany as communism was ending. She called Will an "opportunist turncoat".
Will makes no attempt to conceal her communist past, which includes membership of a workers' militia and academic dissertations steeped in the Marxist ideology of class struggle.
She joined the communist party at the age of 20, and as part of her legal studies spent a year in the Soviet Union -- a classic stepping-stone to a career in the communist "apparat".
She became a law professor at East Berlin's Humboldt University in 1989, two months before the Berlin Wall fell.
That October Will co-wrote a manifesto urging the communist party to reform itself and allow multi-party elections.
Her defenders say this shows her reformist credentials, civil rights activists point to a passage saying opposition groups should be suppressed in certain circumstances.
Will herself has made few comments, except to say that she has completely changed her views and learned to respect the rule of law as "a value in itself".
Wolfgang Birthler, head of the SPD in the state assembly, said his party had "fulfilled its aim of excluding no one merely because of their East German (communist) past".
But Peter Hintze, general secretary of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative Christian Democrats in Bonn, said:

"Rosemarie Will, who belonged to the so-called combat troops of the working class' to suppress opponents of the regime, has no moral right to supervise courts dealing with the consequences of East German injustice."
